opus-5.5.text:
I think the hardest part is that "useful" is only obvious in hindsight. When you start a project, you're really betting on what the field will care about a year or two later, and most of the signals you get in the moment are noisy. Many papers chase what's trendy right now, and by the time the work is done, the problem has either been solved by scale or simply stopped mattering.

For me, a few things have helped. First, I try to look for problems where there's a real tension that won't go away by itself. In my area, efficient sequence modeling, that tension is between expressiveness and efficiency. Transformers are powerful, but attention's cost grows quadratically with context length, and as people push toward longer contexts and more inference-time compute, that cost only becomes more painful. So working on linear attention or recurrent-style architectures felt like betting on a constraint that would keep getting tighter, not looser.

Second, I care a lot about whether an idea can actually run fast on real hardware. A lot of architectures look elegant on paper but never get adopted because they can't be trained efficiently on GPUs. So a big part of my work has been designing algorithms that are hardware-aware, for example finding chunkwise parallel forms so these models can use matrix multiplications and tensor cores. If you ignore that side, you can solve a problem in theory that nobody can use in practice.

Third, it's about taste, and taste mostly comes from doing a lot of experiments and reading old literature. Many of the ideas we revisit, like the delta rule or fast weight programmers, are decades old. The useful question is often not "what's totally new" but "what was previously impractical that we can now make work at scale."

The last challenge is psychological. Unglamorous problems often matter most, like a kernel implementation or a stable parameterization. You need some confidence to keep working on something when it isn't getting attention yet. But if you believe the underlying constraint is real, I think that patience usually pays off.

r001.rationale: The response does not claim that clear goals lead researchers to encounter few setbacks.

r002.rationale: It says usefulness is often clear only in hindsight and calls choosing a useful problem the hardest part, but does not clearly compare that challenge with solving technical problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest challenge is distinguishing between problems that feel important and problems that actually are important, and the gap between those two is often much larger than people expect.

When I was starting out, I was drawn to whatever was trending. In the Transformer era, that meant chasing attention variants, trying to squeeze another half point out of a benchmark. It felt productive because everyone around you is working on it and there's immediate feedback. But in hindsight a lot of that work got erased within a year. Not because it was wrong, but because the field moved and those marginal gains didn't compound into anything.

What I eventually realized, working on linear attention and later on things like Gated DeltaNet and the hardware-aware kernels in flash-linear-attention, is that a good research problem usually sits at the intersection of three things. First, there's a real bottleneck that won't go away by just scaling up. For me that was the quadratic cost of attention and the KV cache at long context. Second, there's a reason why the obvious solutions have failed, and you have some new angle on why. For linear attention, the early versions just didn't match softmax attention in quality, and understanding that gap as a question of memory capacity and update rules, not just a kernel choice, opened up a whole line of work. Third, and this is the part people underestimate, it has to be something you can actually iterate on with the resources you have. A beautiful idea you can only test at a scale you'll never reach is not a research problem, it's a wish.

The hard part is that these three conditions rarely line up at the same time, and when they do it often looks unfashionable. Linear attention was quite a cold topic for a while. People thought it was settled, that it just didn't work. Working on something that others have written off requires a kind of stubbornness, and you have to be honest with yourself about whether that stubbornness is insight or just denial.

So if I had to summarize, the biggest challenge is having enough taste to recognize a bottleneck that matters, enough depth to understand why it hasn't been solved, and enough patience to stay with it while it's unpopular. Taste is the part you can't shortcut. It comes from reading a lot, implementing a lot, and being wrong many times, so that you develop a feel for which directions actually have room to grow.

r001.rationale: The response describes conditions that make research problems hard to choose, but it does not claim researchers encounter few setbacks when their goals are clear.

r002.rationale: It identifies recognizing which problems matter as the biggest challenge, but does not compare that challenge with solving technical problems or say it is greater.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest challenge is figuring out whether a problem is actually important, rather than just interesting or easy to formulate. Once you have a clear problem, you can start trying methods and measuring progress. But choosing the problem means asking: if we solve this, what changes? Who can do something they couldn’t do before?

There’s also a tension between importance and tractability. You want to work on something that matters, but you need a way to make progress and learn from the results. I think a useful approach is to keep a big question in mind, then find a smaller problem whose solution would genuinely teach you something about it. The danger is that the smaller problem becomes the goal, and you forget why you started.

r001.rationale: The response says that once a problem is clear, researchers can try methods and measure progress, but it does not claim they encounter few setbacks when their goals are clear.

r002.rationale: It presents choosing whether a problem matters as the biggest challenge and treats trying methods as a later step, communicating that problem selection is a greater challenge than technical problem-solving.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest challenge is separating a problem that is interesting to solve from a problem that is actually worth solving. As researchers, we’re drawn to questions where we can see a path forward. But that can lead us to choose a problem because we have the tools for it, rather than because the answer would matter.

A useful question to ask is: if we solved this completely, what would change? Would someone be able to do something they couldn’t do before? Would it change how we understand a broader problem? If that’s hard to explain, maybe we haven’t found the right question yet.

Of course, you can’t know the impact in advance. So the challenge is to develop good judgment while staying willing to revise your assumptions as you learn.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing problems that matter, but does not claim researchers encounter few setbacks when they are clear about what they want to accomplish.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes interesting problems from worthwhile ones, but does not compare uncertainty about what is useful to build with solving technical problems.
